title: the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma
tomorrow: a sprout, a bird, an elephant, a god. what do they share?

segments.voice: Yesterday in the four mahavakyas, a question asked twice: who is this one? The answer pointed past the eye to prajnana, the knowing that never gets seen. Today, what that knowing is.

Two people read the same text message and come away sure of opposite things. Same words, same punctuation, and a whole evening of argument about what the sender meant. The Aitareya's great saying has had that kind of evening for a very long time. Prajnanam brahma: the knowing is Brahman. So is the knowing in me Brahman? Two great teachers of Vedanta read the very same two Sanskrit words, and land in different places.
screen: `ONE TEXT, TWO READINGS.` → `THE KNOWING IS BRAHMAN.` → `IS THE KNOWING IN ME BRAHMAN?`

segments.voice: Shankara, the teacher of Advaita, reads it straight. The knowing in a person and Brahman are one, without a second. What feels like a separate knower, a small self with its own little light, is a misreading. When it's seen through, nothing new is gained; the knowing was Brahman all along. His strongest point: the Aitareya walks back from the thing, to the sense, to the knowing, and then simply says, the knowing is Brahman. Not is like. Not lives in. Is. Ramanuja reads the same words another way. For him, the self that knows is real and distinct, and Brahman dwells within it as its inner ruler, the self of the self. Saying the knowing is Brahman is true the way pointing at a body names the person living in it. His strongest point: the Upanishads also speak of Brahman as the inner controller who dwells within all beings, and as the Lord to be loved; a real knower remains, to know and to love. Both teachers hold the Upanishad as true. Both read it closely. In Sanskrit the saying is just two words side by side, with no is between them; English supplies it. The teachers part over what that missing is is doing: the same as, or the indwelling of. Both readings are still taught, each with its own teachers and its own devotion. The Aitareya doesn't settle it for them, and this lesson doesn't either.
screen: `SHANKARA: ONE, WITHOUT A SECOND.` · `THE SEPARATE KNOWER: A MISREADING.` · `RAMANUJA: BRAHMAN, THE INNER RULER.` · `A REAL KNOWER, TO KNOW AND TO LOVE.` · then, large: `WHAT DOES IS DO?`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write the saying twice. Once as Shankara hears it: the knowing is Brahman, one without a second. Once as Ramanuja hears it: Brahman dwells within the knower as its inner self. Read both lines slowly, and stay longest with the one you didn't expect to like.
The four mahavakyas, and prajnanam brahma heard two ways: one without a second, or Brahman dwelling within the one who knows.
Here's the line: the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma, one sentence and two careful readings. Day 1739, done.

howItsDone: Students in each Vedanta school study the great sayings through their own school's commentaries, so prajnanam brahma is taught with Shankara as the guide in Advaita and with Ramanuja in Sri Vaishnava communities.

fork.setup: your study partner reads prajnanam brahma Shankara's way and asks you for the other side's best case. what do you give?
options: the Upanishads also call Brahman the inner ruler within beings; a real knower remains to love.
Ramanuja simply didn't read the Sanskrit as carefully as Shankara did.
the other side says the saying is only poetry and makes no claim.
fork.reveal: Ramanuja reads the same line closely: Brahman dwells within a real, distinct self as its inner ruler, the self of the self. Both readings are still taught.

original.note: Sanskrit prajnanam brahma, the knowing is Brahman: the Aitareya's great saying, read in more than one way.

trapdoor: what you thought: a great saying has one meaning everyone in the tradition shares.
what it means: Shankara hears one without a second; Ramanuja hears Brahman as the inner self of a real knower.
what a scholar hears: Advaita reads the sentence as identity; Vishishtadvaita reads the self as Brahman's body with Brahman its inner ruler, the antaryamin of Brihadaranyaka 3.7.

chat.meaning: Shankara reads prajnanam brahma as one without a second; Ramanuja reads Brahman as the inner self dwelling in a real, distinct knower.

Shankara.meaning: a teacher of Advaita Vedanta and commentator on the Upanishads

Ramanuja.meaning: a teacher of Vishishtadvaita Vedanta, revered in Sri Vaishnava tradition

Advaita.meaning: non-duality; the Vedanta school of Shankara

prajnanam brahma.meaning: the knowing is Brahman; one of the great sayings

Vedanta.meaning: schools of thought built on the Upanishads

sources.ref: Shankara, commentary on the Aitareya Upanishad (the saying read as identity; the separate knower as a superimposition removed by knowledge)
Ramanuja, Vedartha Sangraha and Sri Bhashya (Brahman as the inner self and ruler of real, distinct selves; the great sayings read accordingly); Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.7 (the inner controller)

notes: Block 'the four mahavakyas — prajnanam brahma', day 5 of 9 (1735–1743). 1735 named the two readings in one paragraph; this day lets each speak at length with its strongest point.

Please check both summaries carefully: Advaita (identity; the separate knower a misreading, nothing gained when seen through) and Vishishtadvaita (the self real and distinct; Brahman its inner ruler; the self as Brahman's body; devotion). They are general characterizations, not quotations; confirm neither is misrepresented or ranked, and that a Sri Vaishnava reader would accept 'saying the knowing is Brahman is true the way pointing at a body names the person living in it'.
The Sanskrit sentence prajnanam brahma is a nominal sentence of two words with no verb; English supplies 'is'. Confirm this grammar note is stated fairly.
